★★★ THE x86_64 COUNTERPART TO `asm_arm64_branch_call` — DELIBERATELY THE SAME PROGRAM, SO THE DIFFERENCES ARE THE DIALECT AND NOTHING ELSE. Same arithmetic (100−7=93, ×2=186, −144=42), same branch structure, same call, same exit code; a different token table, a different operand order, a different memory syntax, different mnemonics. Reading the two `main.s` files side by side IS the evidence that a dialect is a language rather than a set of knobs — and running both is the evidence that the shared line grammar serves both without knowing which it has.

★★★ WHAT THIS FILE WITNESSES THAT ITS arm64 SIBLING CANNOT: MEMORY OPERANDS AND THE OVERLOADED MNEMONIC, WHICH ARE THE SAME FACT. `movq` here is THREE different DSS opcodes and the walker must elect between them from the operand shape alone:
  • `movq $100, %rax`            → `mov`   (immediate)
  • `movq %rax, 40(%rsp)`        → `store` (memory is the destination)
  • `movq 40(%rsp), %rdx`        → `load`  (memory is the source)
  • `movq %rdx, (%rsp,%r8,8)`    → `store`, base + index*scale form
  • `movq (%rsp,%r8,8), %r9`     → `load`,  base + index*scale form
One spelling, three opcodes, five encodings. That is why `instructions[]` rows carry an ARRAY of opcode names and why the election is the TARGET's job (`encoding.variants[].guard.operandKinds`) rather than the dialect's — a dialect that named the winner per shape would be a second, drifting copy of the target's guard table. ⓘ arm64 needs none of this: it spells the three `mov`/`ldr`/`str`, so its rows are singletons. WHICH mnemonics are overloaded is a DIALECT property, which is an independent argument for the array living here.

★★ AND THE TWO `result: none` OPCODES IN THIS FILE DISAGREE ABOUT OPERAND ORDER, WHICH IS THE SUBTLEST THING IT PINS. `cmpq $93, %rax` must become LIR `[rax, imm 93]` — the written order REVERSED, because LIR's `cmp` takes the LHS first and AT&T writes the LHS last. `movq %rax, 40(%rsp)` must become LIR `[rax, rsp, MemBase, MemOffset]` — the written order PRESERVED, because LIR's `store` takes the stored VALUE first. Both are `destinationLast`; both produce no value; no positional rule gets both right. Placement therefore has to be matched by KIND against the elected variant's `operandKinds`, and getting it wrong is a silent miscompile in one direction (a reversed compare flips a branch) and a verifier error in the other (`lir_verifier` independently requires MemBase then MemOffset to be the last two operands).

★★ EVERY EDGE HAS A DISTINCT WRONG ANSWER, so a dropped one cannot hide behind a coincidence:
  • `jne Lfail` wrongly taken (cond-code table reversed) ⇒ exit 1;
  • `je Lwin` wrongly not taken (jcc taken/fallthrough operands transposed) ⇒ falls into `jmp Lfail` ⇒ exit 1;
  • the unlabeled fallthrough block dropped ⇒ the multiply never runs ⇒ exit 1;
  • the STORE dropped, or the LOAD reading a different slot ⇒ `cmpq $186, %rdx` fails ⇒ exit 1;
  • the index*scale form computing `[rsp+6]` instead of `[rsp+48]` (scale ignored) ⇒ a misaligned read of the wrong bytes ⇒ not 42;
  • `call helper` dropped, or its result ignored ⇒ exit 186;
  • `subq %rcx, %rax` read as destination-FIRST ⇒ helper computes `144-186` and writes rcx ⇒ not 42.

★ THE FRAME IS HAND-WRITTEN BECAUSE THAT IS WHAT THE `encode` TIER MEANS. `subq $72, %rsp` / `addq $72, %rsp` is the programmer's own prologue and epilogue; `materializeCallingConvention` does not run at this tier, by design, because injecting a second prologue over it is a miscompile of intent. 72 is not arbitrary: it leaves `%rsp` 16-byte aligned at the `call` (the return address pushed into `main` made it ≡8 mod 16), and both memory slots — `40(%rsp)` and `(%rsp,%r8,8)` = `[rsp+48]` — sit ABOVE the 32-byte region Win64 reserves as shadow space for a callee, so the same file is correct under both ABIs.
★ ONLY REGISTERS THAT ARE VOLATILE UNDER *BOTH* ABIs ARE TOUCHED — rax, rcx, rdx, r8, r9. ⚠ rsi/rdi would have been the natural choice on System V and are CALLEE-SAVED on Win64; using them would have produced a fixture that passed on Linux and corrupted the trampoline's state on Windows, which is exactly the kind of one-leg-green result this corpus exists to prevent.

★ WHY THE BRANCH TARGETS ARE `Lwin`/`Lfail` AND NOT gas's USUAL `.L1`/`.L2`: a leading `.` is this dialect's `directiveIntroducer`, so `.L1:` routes to `asmDirective` and the trailing colon has nowhere to go. Plain identifiers are equally valid gas. Anchored: D-ASM-DOT-PREFIXED-LOCAL-LABELS-UNPARSEABLE.

★★ TWO OBJECT FORMATS FROM ONE FILE, which is the claim the sibling `asm_arith_return42` already makes and this one extends to memory and calls: pe64 and elf64 share the dialect and the register file but differ in object format, entry trampoline, image layout and — for the `call` — relocation kind. One `.s` proving both is a real cross-format claim, not a repetition.

★ THE `release` ARM, SCOPED HONESTLY. At the `encode` tier no MIR module exists, so the optimizer, the register allocator and calling-convention materialization never run — this arm does NOT witness the optimizer and cannot. It pins the narrower fact that `--config=release` still produces a working binary, i.e. the release configuration does not BREAK the assembly path. What keeps a `.s` out of the optimizer is structural (`pipelineEntry` + no MIR module to run passes over), not this arm.
